simple: a push or a pull, with a size and a direction.
analogy: Amara's arms pushing the tray.
precise: a vector quantity that changes the motion of a body; measured in newtons (N), where 1 N accelerates 1 kg by 1 m/s². Forces on one body add as vectors (MA201 F0-47).
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); U1 of F10-01 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the total push on a thing decides how quickly its speed changes.
analogy: push the tray harder than the glasses weigh and it speeds up upwards.
precise: for a body of constant mass m, the vector sum of the forces equals m times the acceleration: ΣF = m a.
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the pull of the Earth on the vehicle.
analogy: the glasses pulling the tray down.
precise: the gravitational force m g, pointing down; this course uses g = 9.81 m/s².
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); V1 of F10-01 (the value g = 9.81 m/s^2 as cited in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the push a spinning propeller makes by throwing air backwards (for a drone: downwards).
analogy: Amara's arms pushing the tray up.
precise: the force a rotor exerts on the vehicle along its spin axis, the reaction to the momentum the rotor gives to the air; on a multirotor each rotor's thrust points along the body's up axis. Not the C++ library of the same name (CU401).
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the push of the air against anything that moves through it.
analogy: the breeze pushing against the tray.
precise: the aerodynamic force component opposite to the velocity relative to the air; this course models the body's drag as k v|v| with an exercise value k.
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-01 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the upward push a wing gets from moving through the air.
analogy: none in the tray story: Amara's tray has no wings (F10-06 adds one).
precise: the aerodynamic force component perpendicular to the oncoming air; for a wing L = ½ ρ V² S CL (F10-06).
source: B1 of F10-01 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the total thrust needed to stay at the same height.
analogy: pushing up exactly as hard as the glasses weigh.
precise: with no vertical acceleration and no vertical drag, the vertical part of the thrust equals the weight: T cos a = m g for a vehicle tilted by a (T = m g when level).
source: D1 of F10-01 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many times the vehicle's weight its rotors can push at most.
analogy: how much more Amara could lift than the full tray weighs.
precise: Tmax / (m g); below 1 the vehicle cannot hover; the margin above 1 is what is left for climbing, tilting and control.
source: D1 of F10-01 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the top speed at which a vehicle climbs with a fixed extra thrust, because drag grows until it uses all of the extra.
analogy: walking into the wind: the faster you go, the harder the wind pushes back.
precise: the speed at which T − m g − k v² = 0, so v = √((T − m g)/k) in this chapter's model.
source: D1 of F10-01 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a multirotor with four rotors at the corners of a square, the nose between two of them.
analogy: Jonas's four fingertips under a square tray.
precise: a multirotor whose four rotor axes are parallel to the body z axis, placed at (±a, ±a) in the body x–y plane, with diagonal rotors spinning in the same direction. This course numbers them 1 front-left, 2 front-right, 3 rear-right, 4 rear-left.
source: B1 of F10-02 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-02 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: tipping sideways, tipping nose up or down, and turning the nose left or right.
analogy: tipping the tray left–right, front–back, and twisting it flat.
precise: rotations about the body x, y and z axes; in DN201's axes (x forward, y left, z up) positive roll lowers the right side, positive pitch lowers the nose, positive yaw turns the nose left (right-hand rule). F10-03 defines the angles.
source: D1 of F10-02 (derivations shown in the chapter); U1 of F10-02 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the twist a spinning propeller gives the body, opposite to its own spin.
analogy: Jonas's fingertip friction, which turns the tray.
precise: the air resists the propeller with a drag torque; the motor must supply an equal torque to keep the speed, and by Newton's third law the body receives the opposite torque about the rotor axis. This course models it as c f, with c = kQ/kT (F10-05).
source: B1 of F10-02 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-02 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule that turns "how much thrust and how much turning" into four motor commands.
analogy: Jonas deciding how hard each fingertip presses.
precise: the inverse of the linear map from rotor forces to total thrust and body torques, f = M^−1 u; DN301 (F10-18) treats it as control allocation with limits.
source: B1 of F10-02 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-02 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much turning the vehicle can produce about an axis before a motor hits its limit.
analogy: tipping the tray is easy, twisting it is hard.
precise: the largest torque about an axis that the mixer can deliver with every rotor force between zero and its maximum, at a given total thrust.
source: D1 of F10-02 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: fewer "pushes" than ways to move.
analogy: Jonas can only push up, so to move the tray sideways he has to tip it.
precise: a rigid body has six degrees of freedom (three of position, three of attitude); a quadrotor has four independent inputs (thrust and three torques), so horizontal motion is reached only through attitude.
source: B1 of F10-02 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how fast the drone is turning about its own three axes, right now.
analogy: how fast Mei's wrist is twisting, felt in her own hand.
precise: the components of the angular velocity vector ω in the body frame: p about body x, q about body y, r about body z, in rad/s; a three-axis gyroscope measures them (plus errors).
source: B1 of F10-03 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how fast the three angles on the screen are changing.
analogy: how fast Mei's three instructions would have to change to follow her wrist.
precise: the time derivatives (φ̇, θ̇, ψ̇); they equal a matrix W(φ, θ) times the body rates (p, q, r), and W contains tan θ and 1/cos θ.
source: B1 of F10-03 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-03 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: for small tilts, the angle rates are about the same as the body rates.
analogy: while the tray is nearly level, twisting your wrist changes the tilt by the same amount.
precise: for |φ|, |θ| ≪ 1 rad, W(φ, θ) ≈ I, so (φ̇, θ̇, ψ̇) ≈ (p, q, r), and sin a ≈ a, cos a ≈ 1; the basis of the simple attitude controllers of DN301.
source: B1 of F10-03 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-03 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an object that does not bend or stretch, so one position and one attitude describe it completely.
analogy: the tray, if the glasses were glued on.
precise: a body in which the distance between any two points is constant; its configuration has six degrees of freedom (three of position, three of attitude).
source: B2 of F10-04 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics"); B1 of F10-04 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how hard it is to start the body turning about each axis.
analogy: the long tray tips easily one way and hardly the other.
precise: the symmetric 3 × 3 matrix J relating angular velocity to angular momentum, L = J ω; in principal axes it is diagonal, J = diag(Jx, Jy, Jz), in kg·m².
source: B2 of F10-04 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the "amount of spin" a body carries.
analogy: a spinning tray that keeps turning after you let go.
precise: L = J ω (body frame for a rigid body about its centre of mass); with no external torque, L expressed in the world frame stays constant.
source: B2 of F10-04 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the two laws that move a rigid body: forces change its velocity, torques change its spin.
analogy: pushing the tray along, and twisting it.
precise: m dv/dt = ΣF (world frame) and J dω/dt + ω × Jω = Στ (body frame, about the centre of mass).
source: B2 of F10-04 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics"); B1 of F10-04 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the rotation law that makes a spinning body wobble and precess even without any torque.
analogy: none in the tray story; think of a spinning book thrown into the air.
precise: the term ω × Jω in J dω/dt + ω × Jω = τ, which appears because J is constant in the body frame while the body frame rotates; it vanishes when ω is along a principal axis.
source: B2 of F10-04 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of numbers that says everything about the vehicle at one instant.
analogy: where the tray is, how fast it moves, how it is tilted and how fast it turns.
precise: here x = (p, v, q, ω, ω1..4): position and velocity (world), unit quaternion, body rates and the four rotor speeds — 17 numbers.
source: D1 of F10-04 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way to step a simulation forward that samples the slope four times per step.
analogy: checking the path at the start, twice in the middle and at the end before taking a step.
precise: xn+1 = xn + h (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4)/6 with the four slope evaluations of MA302 F0-76; a fourth-order method.
source: U1 of F10-04 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: Thrust coefficient kT and torque coefficient kQ
simple: two numbers that say how much push and how much drag-twist a propeller gives at a given speed.
analogy: how much the tray rises, and how much Priya's wrist is twisted, per effort.
precise: the constants of the static propeller model T = kT ω² (N) and Q = kQ ω² (N·m), valid for a given propeller in still air; found by measurement.
source: B1 of F10-05 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-05 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a steady condition, and a straight-line description of small changes around it.
analogy: how Priya's arms respond to one more glass when the tray is already full.
precise: an equilibrium (here a steady rotor speed ω0); replacing the non-linear model by its first-order Taylor expansion around ω0 gives a first-order linear system with time constant τ (RB202, MA301).
source: D1 of F10-05 (derivations shown in the chapter); U1 of F10-05 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Thrust coefficient kT and torque coefficient kQ

simple: how long the rotor takes to cover most of a change in speed.
analogy: the moment the tray dips before Priya's arms catch up.
precise: for small steps around ω0, τ = Jr / (KtKe/R + 2 kQ ω0); after τ the speed has covered 63.2 % of the step.
source: D1 of F10-05 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Thrust coefficient kT and torque coefficient kQ

simple: a rig that holds a motor and propeller still and measures the push and the speed.
analogy: weighing how hard Priya can push up on a bathroom scale.
precise: a fixture with a load cell (and often a torque sensor) that records thrust, torque, speed, voltage and current at a series of commands, from which kT, kQ and efficiency are fitted.
source: B1 of F10-05 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Thrust coefficient kT and torque coefficient kQ

simple: choosing a model's number so that it misses the measurements as little as possible, and the misses themselves.
analogy: drawing the best smooth line through bumpy marks.
precise: the parameter that minimises the sum of squared differences between data and model; for T = k ω², k = Σ Tj ωj² / Σ ωj⁴; residual = measured − model.
source: D1 of F10-05 (derivations shown in the chapter); U1 of F10-05 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Thrust coefficient kT and torque coefficient kQ

simple: the upward push of moving air on a wing, and a number saying how good the wing is at it at that moment.
analogy: the breeze pushing Nadia's tilted tray up.
precise: L = ½ ρ V² S CL, with air density ρ, airspeed V, wing area S and lift coefficient CL, which grows with the angle of attack up to a maximum CL,max. Lift itself was defined in F10-01.
source: B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); U1 of F10-06 (university chapters cited for what they teach) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much the wing is tipped up against the air coming at it.
analogy: how far Nadia raises the tray's front edge.
precise: the angle between the wing's reference line (chord) and the direction of the oncoming air; CL rises roughly in proportion to it until the stall.
source: B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the wing is tipped too far, the air stops following it and the lift drops.
analogy: the tray tipped too far, flapping.
precise: flow separation above a critical angle of attack, at which CL reaches CL,max and then falls; the stall speed in level flight is Vs = √(2W/(ρ S CL,max)).
source: B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-06 (derivations shown in the chapter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a formula saying how much drag comes with each amount of lift.
analogy: the harder the breeze lifts the tray, the harder it also pushes it back.
precise: CD = CD0 + k CL², a parasite part CD0 and an induced part k CL² that comes with making lift.
source: B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many newtons of lift a wing gives per newton of drag.
analogy: how much the breeze lifts the tray for each bit it pushes back.
precise: L/D = CL/CD; with the drag polar its maximum is 1/(2√(CD0k)) at CL = √(CD0/k).
source: D1 of F10-06 (derivations shown in the chapter); B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how steeply the aircraft climbs or sinks, and how far a glider travels forwards per metre it sinks.
analogy: the slope of the garden path Nadia walks down.
precise: the flight-path angle γ is the angle of the velocity above the horizontal (negative when descending); in a steady glide tan(−γ) = D/L, so the glide ratio equals L/D.
source: D1 of F10-06 (derivations shown in the chapter); B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far the wings are tilted in a turn, and how many times its weight the wing must lift.
analogy: the tray leaned into the corner, and the glasses pressing in harder.
precise: in a level turn with bank φ, L cos φ = W, so the load factor n = L/W = 1/cos φ; the turn radius is V²/(g tan φ).
source: D1 of F10-06 (derivations shown in the chapter); B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an aircraft that can take off straight up like a multirotor and then fly on wings like an aeroplane.
analogy: Nadia lifting the tray straight up at the bar, then walking fast so the breeze helps.
precise: a class of aircraft that combine powered lift for take-off, hover and landing with wing-borne cruise; the change between the two is the transition. Common layouts: tailsitter, tiltrotor, quadplane (separate lift and cruise propulsion).
source: B1 of F10-06 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
